name: Cyber Threat Intelligence - Best Practices and Maturity Levels

questions.heading: Depth of Threat Intelligence
questions.subheading: What level of intelligence (relative to the Pyramid of Pain) is being used to track adversaries?

recommendations: Automate IOC ingestion: Connect your SIEM/SOAR to curated threat feeds — government and ISAC sources over high-volume commercial feeds.
Establish IOC triage criteria: Define which indicators trigger automatic blocks, which generate analyst alerts, and which are discarded. Undocumented triage leads to alert fatigue.
choices.levelGoal: Establish automated IOC collection and triage. The organization moves from no indicator tracking to a functional ingestion pipeline with criteria defining which indicators trigger blocks, which generate alerts, and which are discarded.

recommendations: Document adversary toolkits: For each tracked tool, record observable characteristics, configurations, and which threat actors use it. This context survives indicator rotation.
Map tools to threat actors and ATT&CK techniques: Document which groups use which tools and what techniques each toolkit enables — the bridge from tool intelligence to behavioral detection.
choices.levelGoal: Add tool-level intelligence to your tracking capability. Build a structured understanding of adversary toolkits, mapping them to threat actors and the ATT&CK techniques they enable — intelligence that remains valid even as specific indicators rotate.

choices.text: Techniques and Tactics used by adversaries
choices.primaryOwner: CTI Lead / Detection Engineering / Red Team
recommendations: Map adversary TTPs to ATT&CK Navigator: Visualize current coverage and prioritize mapping on adversaries most likely to target your organization. Share the heatmap with security leadership.
Build structured threat actor profiles: For each priority adversary, document typical technique sequences, preferred execution contexts, and observed variations.
choices.levelGoal: Add TTP-level intelligence to your tracking capability. Map adversary techniques and tactics to ATT&CK and build structured threat actor profiles — intelligence durable enough to drive detection coverage, hunt hypotheses, and test planning.

recommendations: Formalize behavioral patterns into a threat actor library: Document the consistent behaviors that persist across intrusion campaigns regardless of tools or infrastructure used.

Corroborate patterns across multiple independent sources: A behavioral claim from a single report is a hypothesis. Convergence across three or more independent sources is a durable intelligence finding.
choices.levelGoal: Add behavioral intelligence to your tracking capability. Identify and formalize the low-variance behavioral patterns that persist even when adversaries change tools and infrastructure — the most defensively durable intelligence tier.

questions.heading: Relevance of Threat Intelligence
questions.subheading: How much does the threat intelligence relate to your organization?

recommendations: Define your organizational threat profile: Document which adversaries are most likely to target your organization based on sector, size, geography, and technology stack. This focuses all subsequent collection.
Join your sector's ISAC and subscribe to government feeds: ISACs provide sector-specific intelligence at minimal cost. Audit existing sources and eliminate those that produce no actionable outputs.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a baseline sourcing practice with sector-specific inputs. Move from unstructured sourcing to a defined threat profile, ISAC membership, and government feed subscriptions — raising intelligence relevance above generic open-source reporting.

recommendations: Contextualize sector intelligence to your environment: For each industry report, explicitly assess which threats apply to your technology stack and attack surface. Discard what doesn't apply.

Define PIRs and develop in-house threat profiling: Document the specific intelligence questions your program must answer. Even a part-time analyst dedicated to contextualizing external intel substantially improves relevance.
choices.levelGoal: Contextualize industry intelligence to your specific environment. Begin translating sector-level reporting into organization-specific relevance by mapping threats to your technology stack, attack surface, and business model.

recommendations: Formalize intelligence production: Document how CTI is produced, reviewed, approved, and distributed. Ensure in-house intelligence directly informs detection priorities, hunt planning, and risk decisions.
Build a feedback loop from operations: Create structured processes for IR, SOC, and detection engineering to return findings to CTI. Operational feedback is the primary quality signal for relevance.
choices.levelGoal: Establish in-house intelligence production. Produce or commission intelligence specific to your environment, with documented production processes and operational feedback loops that make the intelligence cycle self-reinforcing.

questions.heading: Operational Integration of Threat Intelligence
questions.subheading: To what extent is threat intelligence integrated across your organization?

choices.text: Reviewed by individuals or siloed teams
recommendations: Map CTI consumer roles: Document who needs intelligence, in what format, and for what purpose. SOC, detection engineering, IR, and leadership each have different requirements.
Establish a monthly cross-functional CTI briefing: A standing meeting with representation from key security functions is the minimum viable integration mechanism.
choices.levelGoal: Break intelligence out of the CTI team silo. Establish distribution channels, define what each consumer function needs, and assign integration champions — so intelligence reaches the teams that act on it.

recommendations: Formalize integration SLAs and measure outputs: Define how quickly each consumer function receives intelligence and in what format. Track detections created from CTI, hunts initiated, and advisories distributed. Low output signals an integration failure.
Establish a CTI working group: A standing cross-functional body with representation from CTI, SOC, detection engineering, and IR formalizes the relationship and surfaces gaps.
choices.levelGoal: Formalize cross-team intelligence workflows. Operate documented SLAs for intelligence hand-offs, a standing cross-functional working group, and measurable indicators of whether integration is producing defensive outputs.

choices.text: Contextualized and made actionable across entire organization
recommendations: Embed CTI in enterprise risk management and board reporting: Intelligence should formally inform risk assessments, investment decisions, and board-level risk reporting on a defined cadence.

Create feedback loops from business to CTI: M&A activity, product launches, and market expansions carry intelligence value. Establish channels for business teams to surface context that enriches threat assessment.
choices.levelGoal: Extend intelligence integration to enterprise decisions. Intelligence formally informs risk management, board-level conversations, and third-party decisions — and feedback from business functions enriches the CTI program in return.

questions.heading: Incorporation of CTI
questions.subheading: How frequently are you incorporating threat intelligence into your organization’s workflows?

recommendations: Assign CTI ownership: Designate one person responsible for monitoring and distributing threat intelligence. Without a named owner, no program will emerge.

Anchor the process to Priority Intelligence Requirements: Define 3–5 specific questions CTI should answer for your organization. PIRs focus initial collection and measure whether the program is delivering value.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI ownership and a minimum viable intake process. Designate responsibility, identify at least one source, and create a basic workflow anchored to Priority Intelligence Requirements — moving from no program to one that produces intermittent operational outputs.

recommendations: Set a fixed monthly CTI review with a standard agenda: Define what gets reviewed each session. Each review must produce at least one documented operational action — a detection update, hunt hypothesis, or advisory.
Track outputs per review cycle: Document what intelligence was reviewed and what action it produced. Cycles that produce no action signal a sourcing or process problem.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a fixed monthly review cadence with documented outputs. A recurring review produces at least one operational action per cycle — a detection update, hunting hypothesis, or SOC advisory.

recommendations: Build a tiered cadence — weekly for operational, monthly for strategic: Active campaign intelligence and sector advisories warrant weekly review. Strategic assessments and threat actor profiles can remain monthly.
Develop Priority Intelligence Requirements: Formally document the intelligence questions your program must answer. PIRs focus collection and measure whether the cadence is producing value.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a tiered weekly-monthly review cadence. High-priority or time-sensitive intelligence is reviewed weekly; strategic intelligence monthly. A PIR list focuses collection on the questions that matter most.

recommendations: Establish daily review for active campaigns and zero-days: Define which intelligence types require daily attention and build a lightweight process that doesn't require full analyst hours.
Define escalation criteria: Document what triggers immediate action vs. standard daily review. Without criteria, daily review becomes noise.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve daily review and action on high-priority intelligence. The most time-sensitive intelligence is reviewed and actioned daily, supported by automation for routine tasks and defined escalation criteria.

questions.heading: Recency of CTI
questions.subheading: How recent is the threat intelligence you use?

recommendations: Audit sources for publication lag: For each source, record how quickly it reports on threat events. Eliminate sources that consistently deliver stale intelligence.

Map PIRs to freshness requirements: Tactical intelligence questions need frequent refresh; strategic questions tolerate longer cycles. Direct recency investment where staleness actually changes decisions.
choices.levelGoal: Move from unknown to annual-or-better recency. Audit sources, establish timestamping standards, map freshness requirements to PIRs, and ensure primary sources publish at monthly frequency or better.

recommendations: Replace annual reports with monthly or more frequent sources: Subscribe to feeds and services that publish current intelligence, not retrospective analysis.

Evaluate each source against its actual reporting lag: Measure how quickly sources report on significant threat developments. A source that reports weeks after an event is not a monthly source regardless of its publication schedule.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve monthly-or-better recency for all primary intelligence. A tiered recency model distinguishes tactical intelligence (refreshed weekly or more) from strategic intelligence (monthly), with source lag measured explicitly.

recommendations: Build a tiered recency model: Tactical intelligence requires weekly or near-real-time refresh; strategic intelligence can be monthly. Apply recency investment where staleness changes decisions.
Establish a formal source ROI review: Semi-annually, assess each source against how often it answered a PIR and generated an operational action. Replace sources that consistently underperform.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve weekly-or-better recency for priority intelligence. Near-real-time monitoring covers the highest-priority threat categories. Staleness is managed automatically and freshness is measured against operational response lag.

questions.heading: Speed of CTI Dissemination
questions.subheading: How quickly is new threat intelligence - either internally created or externally sourced - processed and disseminated within your organization?

recommendations: Create a dissemination channel and produce a monthly threat summary: A 1–2 page summary of the current threat landscape relevant to your sector is the minimum viable intelligence product.
Differentiate formats by audience: SOC analysts need IOCs and technique alerts; leadership needs risk framing and business context. One format serving all audiences serves none well.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a dissemination channel and monthly cadence reaching defined consumers. Formats are differentiated across strategic, operational, and tactical audiences. Effectiveness is tracked to identify where the chain breaks down.

recommendations: Establish weekly dissemination to operational consumers: SOC, detection engineering, and IR benefit from more frequent updates. A weekly advisory for high-priority items is achievable without significant additional effort.
Build an emergency dissemination path: Active campaigns and zero-days cannot wait for scheduled reporting. Define a fast-track process for critical intelligence that reaches consumers within hours.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve weekly dissemination to operational consumers. An emergency path handles time-critical intelligence outside the standard cycle. Dissemination-to-action latency is measured.

recommendations: Automate IOC and time-critical alert distribution via SOAR and ticketing systems: Automated dissemination eliminates manual steps and reduces lag for structured intelligence.
Define escalation criteria for same-day distribution: Not all intelligence warrants daily push. Document what triggers immediate notification vs. standard daily cadence.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve daily dissemination with automated workflows. Automated pipelines handle IOCs and time-critical alerts. Quality gates ensure speed does not degrade the accuracy of what is disseminated.

questions.heading: CTI Driven Decision Making
questions.subheading: To what extent is CTI incorporated into decision making?

choices.text: CTI is considered, but not a driving factor
recommendations: Require CTI input on security investment decisions: Starting with the next planning cycle, CTI analysis must accompany major security investment proposals.
Build a threat-to-investment mapping: Connect current defensive investments to the adversaries most likely to target your organization. Coverage gaps become visible and justify future investment.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI as a formal input to security decisions. Designate CTI as a required input to security planning, audit recent decisions for threat context, and build a threat-to-investment mapping connecting defensive spend to the most relevant adversaries.

choices.text: CTI is strongly weighted for cybersecurity decisions
recommendations: Give CTI a formal seat in security architecture reviews: Threat-uninformed architecture creates gaps that are expensive to close after deployment. CTI input before design finalization is far more effective.

Adopt your organization's risk language: Translate threat intelligence into the terms your risk function uses — probability, business impact, control effectiveness. Intelligence framed in risk language is actionable in investment decisions.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI as a weighted factor in cybersecurity decisions. CTI analysis is formally required in security investment documentation and the CTI function has a seat in security architecture reviews.

choices.text: CTI is strongly weighted for cybersecurity and business decisions
recommendations: Build executive threat briefing capability: Translate intelligence into business impact language — revenue at risk, operational disruption scenarios, regulatory exposure. Brief the CISO and board on a defined cadence.

Connect CTI to M&A, vendor selection, and strategic planning: High-impact business decisions carry implicit cyber risk. A lightweight process for CTI input before decisions are finalized prevents expensive surprises.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI as a driver of executive-level and business decisions. Intelligence informs board and risk committee conversations in business impact language, connects to M&A and vendor selection, and is expressed in the organization's risk framework vocabulary.

name: Defensive Measures - Best Practices and Maturity Levels

questions.heading: Data Collection
questions.subheading: To what extent is data collected, stored, and accessible?

choices.text: Logs are collected and stored for at least 90 days
choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA, T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), T.4 (SOAR), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Document and enforce 90-day retention for critical systems: Formalize retention policies, get CISO approval, and verify compliance across all critical log sources.

Test log retrieval under realistic conditions: Retained logs that can't be efficiently queried under investigation pressure have limited value. Validate retrieval time and completeness before declaring this operational.
choices.levelGoal: Establish 90-day log retention as a baseline. Logs from critical systems are retained for at least 90 days with documented, CISO-approved policies and validated retrieval performance.

choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA, T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), T.4 (SOAR), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Implement a consistent log tagging taxonomy: Define tags that follow a documented schema and apply them uniformly. Inconsistent tagging defeats the purpose of indexing.
Align tags to ATT&CK data sources and audit completeness: Verify every active log source is tagged. Gaps in the taxonomy create blind spots in hunting and investigation workflows.
choices.levelGoal: Implement consistent log tagging aligned to ATT&CK data sources. A documented taxonomy ensures all log sources are tagged and completeness is audited, enabling analysts and hunters to filter by log type with confidence.

choices.text: Logs are collected from multiple sensor types
choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA, T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), T.4 (SOAR), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Extend coverage to cloud, endpoint, network, identity, and OT/ICS: Map current log sources to ATT&CK data source categories. Gaps in the map are gaps in detection and hunting capability.
Automate sensor health monitoring and prioritize new sensors by CTI: A sensor that silently stops logging creates false confidence. Use threat actor TTPs to determine which sensor types to add next.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve comprehensive multi-sensor coverage mapped to ATT&CK. Logs span cloud, endpoint, network, identity, and applicable OT/ICS environments, with sensor health monitored automatically and new sensor priorities driven by CTI.

questions.heading: Risk Assessments
questions.subheading: To what extent are risk assessments performed and operationally useful to your organization?

choices.text: Perform formal risk assessments at least annually
recommendations: Conduct at least one formal risk assessment annually with CTI input: Brief the assessment team on the current threat landscape before each cycle. CTI-uninformed assessments miss the most operationally relevant risks.
Connect every finding to an owner and remediation target: Findings without documented owners and timelines accumulate without closure. The assessment is only as valuable as the action it drives.
choices.levelGoal: Establish annual formal risk assessments with CTI input. At least one formal assessment is conducted annually, with CTI informing the threat landscape context and findings connected to documented operational priorities.

choices.text: Results are used operationally, with measures taken to harden security posture based on findings
recommendations: Build a finding-to-remediation tracking process: Every finding needs an owner, target date, and progress mechanism. Without tracking, findings accumulate without closure.
Prioritize remediations by threat relevance and business impact: Use CTI and business context to sequence effort. Measure risk reduction over time and report trend direction to leadership.
choices.levelGoal: Make assessment findings operationally consequential. A tracking process assigns owners and target dates to each finding, remediations are prioritized by impact and complexity, and risk reduction is measured and reported over time.

choices.text: Assessment is focused on metrics and assets tailored to the organization’s need, informed by CTI team
recommendations: Develop a repeatable threat-informed assessment methodology: Document how CTI informs scoping and threat scenario development. Consistency enables year-over-year comparisons and tracks improvement.
Maintain a living threat-to-asset mapping: Connect priority threat actors to the assets they most likely target. Use this to focus assessment scope and communicate risk prioritization to leadership.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a repeatable, threat-informed assessment methodology. CTI formally informs assessment scoping, a living threat-to-asset mapping drives inputs, and findings connect directly to the security roadmap and budget.

questions.heading: Attack Surface Scoping
questions.subheading: To what extent is your attack surface mapped out, understood and prioritized?

choices.cmm_v2: S.7 (Log Management), T.3 (EDR), Pr.2 (Operationsand Facilities), T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR)
S.7 (Log Management), T.3 (EDR), Pr.2 (Operationsand Facilities), T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR)
recommendations: Create a critical asset inventory with business stakeholder input: Document the systems, data, and services whose compromise would have the highest business impact. Business stakeholders identify crown jewels that technical teams miss.

Use a simple, scalable format: A structured document mapping business functions to supporting systems and entry points is sufficient to start. Begin, then iterate — the map has value before it's complete.
choices.levelGoal: Create a structured inventory of the organization's attack surface. Key assets and exposure points are documented, business stakeholders have identified crown jewels, and highest-exposure components are identified.

choices.text: Attack Surfaces are mapped and periodically reviewed
choices.cmm_v2: S.7 (Log Management), T.3 (EDR), Pr.2 (Operationsand Facilities), T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR)
recommendations: Establish an owner and a quarterly review cadence: Assign accountability for keeping the surface map current. Review on a schedule and trigger additional reviews when significant IT changes occur.
Integrate with change management: New systems, cloud migrations, and acquisitions should trigger a surface review, not wait for the next scheduled cycle.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a maintained, change-management-integrated attack surface map. The map is reviewed on a defined cadence, significant IT changes trigger surface reviews, and defensive priorities are informed by the map.

choices.text: Attack Surfaces are mapped and prioritized periodically
choices.cmm_v2: S.7 (Log Management), T.3 (EDR), Pr.2 (Operationsand Facilities), T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR)
recommendations: Score the attack surface by threat actor relevance and business impact: During each review, rate components against current adversary targeting patterns, exploitability, and business impact if compromised.
Build an executive view of threat-weighted exposure: Translate the prioritized technical inventory into a risk-framed view that enables investment conversations with leadership.
choices.levelGoal: Add threat-informed prioritization to the attack surface map. Each surface area is scored by threat actor relevance, exploitability, and business impact. CTI drives re-prioritization when the threat landscape shifts.

questions.heading: Detection Rules
questions.subheading: How does your organization manage detection rules?

recommendations: Evaluate rules before enabling and document what's deployed: Review imported rules for relevance. Build an inventory tracking which rules are active, when last reviewed, and whether they generate alerts.

Prioritize imports by threat actor relevance: Enable rules that map to ATT&CK techniques used by adversaries most likely to target your organization. Targeted coverage is more valuable than generic volume.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a curated detection rule import practice. Rules are evaluated before enabling, an inventory with effectiveness tracking exists, and imports are prioritized by threat actor relevance and ATT&CK technique mapping.

recommendations: Establish a quarterly tuning cadence: Detection rules degrade as environments and adversary behaviors evolve. Schedule reviews to retire stale rules and refresh relevant ones.
Document every tuning decision: Record what was changed, why, and when. Undocumented tuning decisions create institutional debt that compounds when team members change.
choices.levelGoal: Establish an environment-adapted, regularly-maintained detection rule library. Imported rules are tuned through a documented process with recorded rationale, and internal rule creation capability is being built.

choices.text: Detection rules are correlated with attack surfaces
recommendations: Map detection coverage to ATT&CK by attack surface component: Identify where technique gaps and high-priority surface areas intersect. These intersections have the highest detection investment return.

Maintain a prioritized detection engineering backlog: A visible, structured backlog organized by attack surface and ATT&CK technique ensures gaps are systematically addressed rather than handled ad hoc.
choices.levelGoal: Correlate detection coverage with the prioritized attack surface. Coverage is mapped to ATT&CK techniques by attack surface component, and a formal backlog prioritizes development at the intersection of high-priority surface and technique gaps.

choices.text: Detection rules are implemented based on business priorities
recommendations: Establish a process for business priority inputs to detection: Security and business leadership should identify which assets and scenarios warrant detection investment.

Maintain a living detection coverage document: A current map of coverage against business-priority assets is the evidence base for communicating detection posture to the board and justifying investment.
choices.levelGoal: Align detection development to business priorities. Detection requirements are derived from business priority inputs, coverage is measured against business-critical assets, and a living coverage document serves as the evidence base for investment decisions.

questions.heading: Detection Rule Metadata
questions.subheading: What metadata are your detection rules annotated with that can help contextualize their alerts?

choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), Pr.4 (Use Case Management), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Implement a metadata template for all rules: Every rule must document what behavior triggers it, why it's suspicious, and what false positive scenarios look like. Write for the analyst triaging at 2am.
Backfill descriptions on existing high-priority rules first: Start with the most frequently triggered and escalated rules. Descriptions reduce analyst decision time under pressure.
choices.levelGoal: Add analyst-facing behavioral descriptions to all detection rules. A standardized template ensures every rule includes what is detected, why it is suspicious, and what legitimate vs. malicious activity looks like.

choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), Pr.4 (Use Case Management), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Track false positive rate, true positive rate, and MTTD per rule: These metrics identify rules generating noise, missing attacks, or detecting too slowly.
Build a detection quality dashboard: Aggregate rule metrics into a view that gives leadership visibility into library health and trending quality. Use declining metrics to justify tuning investment.
choices.levelGoal: Add quantitative quality metrics to all detection rules. False positive rate, true positive rate, MTTD, and alert volume are tracked per rule, aggregated in a quality dashboard, and used to drive rule retirement and improvement decisions.

choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), Pr.4 (Use Case Management), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Map all active rules to ATT&CK and visualize in ATT&CK Navigator: Coverage gaps between CTI-tracked techniques and detected techniques are immediate detection engineering priorities.
Use the coverage map to drive detection development: The gap between what adversaries do and what you detect should shrink each quarter. Track delta as a security posture improvement metric.
choices.levelGoal: Map all detection rules to ATT&CK and relevant frameworks. ATT&CK Navigator visualizes coverage gaps, mapping drives detection development priorities, and unmapped CTI-tracked techniques are surfaced as explicit detection gaps.

choices.text: Associated malware, threat groups, or campaigns
choices.cmm_v2: T.1 (SIEM/UEBA), T.2 (NDR), T.3 (EDR), Pr.4 (Use Case Management), S.7 (Log Management)
recommendations: Tag detection rules to specific threat actors, malware families, and campaigns: Actor associations enable rapid detection prioritization when intelligence identifies active adversary activity.

Keep associations current as intelligence evolves: A rule tagged to an outdated threat actor profile is misleading. Assign ownership for maintaining associations as part of the regular CTI-to-detection workflow.
choices.levelGoal: Associate detection rules with specific threat actors, malware families, and campaigns. Associations are maintained as intelligence evolves and enable rapid detection prioritization during active campaigns.

questions.heading: Propagation between CTI and Detections
questions.subheading: How long does it take on average to ingest new intelligence into your detection ruleset?

recommendations: Define a documented CTI-to-detection workflow: Specify how new intelligence flows from CTI to detection engineering — trigger criteria, communication channel, and expected response timeframe.
Establish a standing joint CTI/detection engineering session: Regular interaction surfaces coverage gaps and builds the relationship that enables faster propagation over time.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a formal CTI-to-detection workflow with defined triggers. A documented process, trigger criteria, and a standing joint CTI/detection engineering session ensure new intelligence has a structured path to the detection ruleset.

recommendations: Create a formal intake process with SLAs: Document how CTI submits detection needs, how requests are prioritized, and what the target turnaround is for high-priority vs. standard requests.
Measure propagation latency and identify the bottleneck: Track time from intelligence identification to detection deployment. Visibility into where the process slows down is required to improve it.
choices.levelGoal: Reduce propagation to within a week for priority intelligence. A formal intake process with SLAs governs detection update requests, high-priority intelligence is expedited, and latency is measured.

recommendations: Build an expedited path for critical intelligence: Active exploitation and sector-targeted advisories should have a defined fast-track that bypasses the standard queue and targets same-day deployment.
Automate IOC-based detection propagation via SOAR or TIP: For structured indicator intelligence, automation eliminates the manual steps that introduce lag and inconsistency.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve within-a-day propagation with partial automation. An expedited path enables same-day detection updates for critical intelligence. IOC-based propagation is partially automated via SOAR or TIP integration.

recommendations: Automate the full CTI-to-detection pipeline for structured intelligence: IOC ingestion, indicator-based rule updates, and blocking actions should require no manual intervention.
Validate propagated detections before production deployment: Speed without quality creates alert fatigue. Automated quality gates prevent the pipeline from degrading analyst trust.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve within-an-hour propagation for structured intelligence. Automation handles the CTI-to-detection pipeline. Emergency criteria address active exploitation. Propagated detections are validated before deployment and outcomes are tracked.

questions.heading: Incident Response
questions.subheading: How does your organization respond to an active threat?

recommendations: Build IR playbooks for your most likely incident types: Focus on scenarios CTI identifies as highest probability. Each playbook should include the adversary TTPs associated with that incident type.
Map IR activities to ATT&CK post-incident: After each incident, characterize adversary techniques observed. This retrospective identifies detection gaps and creates a feedback loop to CTI.
choices.levelGoal: Establish playbook-based IR with CTI incorporated into post-incident analysis. IR playbooks cover common incident types, activities are mapped to ATT&CK, and structured retrospectives produce documented lessons learned.

choices.text: Playbook-enabled, some automation for lower-level or repeated threats
recommendations: Develop threat actor-specific playbooks for priority adversaries: Document their known TTPs, typical post-compromise behaviors, and recommended containment approach. Generic playbooks leave gaps that actor-specific intelligence can close.
Run CTI-informed tabletop exercises: Simulations built around current adversary TTPs reveal playbook gaps before incidents do. At minimum one per year with CTI and test team participation.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI-integrated playbooks with threat actor context. Playbooks embed threat actor context, threat actor-specific playbooks exist for priority adversaries, and tabletop exercises incorporate current CTI.

choices.text: Responsive actions are informed by knowledge of likely threat actors and expected TTPs
recommendations: Pre-position IR resources when CTI identifies active campaigns: When intelligence indicates active targeting of your sector, activate preparation — don't wait for the alert.

Build adversary-specific IR dossiers for priority threats: Maintain a current document covering known TTPs, persistence mechanisms, and lateral movement patterns. This reduces decision latency at the most critical moment.
choices.levelGoal: Establish anticipatory IR driven by current CTI. IR resources are pre-positioned when CTI identifies active campaigns. Adversary-specific IR dossiers give responders immediate situational context at incident onset.

questions.heading: Incident Recovery and Forensics
questions.subheading: How does your organization recover from adverse incidents?

choices.text: Ad-hoc or informal digital forensics capabilities
Documented and standardized forensic processes in place
recommendations: Document forensic investigation procedures for common incident types: Cover evidence collection, imaging, and chain of custody. Undocumented processes produce incomplete or inadmissible evidence.

Designate and train forensic leads: Two or more team members should have foundational forensic training and be named as first-call resources. Skills built under non-emergency conditions are far more effective.
choices.levelGoal: Establish standardized forensic processes with CTI integration and a findings repository. Forensic investigations include a structured step to compare findings against current threat intelligence. A forensic findings repository enables pattern recognition across investigations.

choices.text: Threat intelligence feeds are used to link forensic findings to specific threat actors/groups
recommendations: Include a CTI correlation step in every forensic investigation: Compare findings against current intelligence before closing. Adversary tools found in one investigation often reappear in the next.

Build a forensic findings repository: Structured documentation across investigations enables pattern recognition. A second incident using the same adversary tooling should trigger an immediate connection to prior analysis.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI-integrated forensics that feeds intelligence back into the CTI program. Forensic findings routinely enrich CTI with new indicators, technique variants, and tool usage. A forensic intelligence product is produced from significant investigations.

questions.heading: Threat Hunting
questions.subheading: How does your organization actively search out threat actors?

choices.text: Ad-hoc or informal threat hunts triggered by observed activity
recommendations: Document every hunt: Every hunt — including ad hoc — requires a record of hypothesis, data sources, findings, and outcome. Undocumented hunts produce no institutional knowledge even when they find nothing.
Schedule at least one planned hunt per quarter: Ad hoc hunts are reactive. Scheduled hunts build methodology and produce proactive discovery.
choices.levelGoal: Establish documented hunt processes and a minimum quarterly cadence. Every hunt is documented with hypothesis, data sources, findings, and outcomes. At least one formally planned hunt per quarter occurs on schedule.

choices.text: Hunts are conducted based on known/reported relevant vulnerabilities
recommendations: Connect CTI directly to hunt hypothesis generation: When CTI identifies adversary TTPs relevant to your environment, generate a hunt hypothesis from it. A formal process ensures intelligence produces operational outputs.

Build an ATT&CK-organized hypothesis library with a path to detection engineering: Organize hypotheses by technique for rapid deployment. Route confirmed undetected activity directly to detection engineering.
choices.levelGoal: Establish CTI-driven hunting with an ATT&CK-organized hypothesis library. A formal process connects CTI findings to hunting hypotheses, enabling rapid deployment when intelligence identifies adversary activity.

choices.text: Formal threat hunts are proactively conducted based on knowledge of likely adversary behaviors
recommendations: Schedule proactive hunts against priority threat actor behaviors: Run formal hunts on a defined cadence based on TTPs of your highest-priority adversaries — don't wait for intelligence triggers.
Track hunting coverage by ATT&CK technique: Map completed hunts to ATT&CK to identify which techniques you've actively hunted against. Coverage gaps are proactive hunting priorities.
choices.levelGoal: Establish proactive, behavioral hunting on a defined regular schedule. Formal proactive hunts run based on priority threat actor behavioral knowledge. Coverage is tracked by ATT&CK technique and drives future prioritization.

questions.heading: Deception
questions.subheading: To what extent does your organization seek to deceive future threats and keep them from useable/valuable data as defined in MITRE Engage?

recommendations: Inventory deception assets and confirm each generates a verified alert: A deception asset that doesn't reliably trigger an alert provides false confidence. Audit, test, and fix or remove anything that doesn't fire.
Document a deception strategy aligned to your threat model: Scattered lures are less effective than assets placed along the paths adversaries use to reach priority systems.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a documented, verified deception asset inventory. All lures are catalogued, alerting is confirmed for each, placement is optimized for adversary lateral movement paths, and a coherent deception strategy is documented.

choices.tooltip: As discussed in NIST SP 800-160 Vol 2, this refers to intentionally spreading disinformation to adversaries (e.g., posting false information about a system to public forums, creating decoy accounts and credentials).
recommendations: Align deception placement to CTI-identified adversary movement patterns: Use intelligence to understand where adversaries are most likely to go and place assets in their path.
Integrate deception alerts into IR workflows as high-priority events: A deception hit is a near-certain true positive. Document the escalation path and test it before you need it.
choices.levelGoal: Establish active deception integrated with IR workflows. A CTI-informed strategy targets the patterns of relevant adversaries. Deception alerts are treated as high-priority IR events. Infrastructure is documented to prevent blue team confusion.

recommendations: Route honeynet findings into the CTI program: First-hand adversary behavior observed in the honeynet is high-quality intelligence unavailable from passive monitoring. Establish a direct pipeline from honeynet observations to CTI analysis.

Build dedicated IR playbooks for honeynet events: Honeynet incidents require a different response calculus — intelligence collection vs. containment. Document the decision framework before the event, not during it.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a full-scale honeynet that feeds the CTI program. Honeynet observations flow into CTI as first-hand intelligence. Dedicated IR playbooks balance collection and containment. Infrastructure is regularly refreshed to maintain realism.

name: Test & Evaluation - Best Practices and Maturity Levels

questions.heading: Test Focus
questions.subheading: What is the focus of your organization’s testing?

choices.text: Testing is compliance-focused, e.g. security control assessment
choices.tooltip: Security control assessments evaluate whether security controls are functioning as intended.
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
recommendations: Add one threat-informed test scenario to each compliance cycle: Compliance testing confirms controls exist; a parallel threat-informed test confirms they work. Start with a scenario targeting your single most likely threat actor.

Map compliance controls to ATT&CK techniques: Identify what each compliance requirement is meant to detect or prevent. This reveals what compliance testing validates and what it misses from a threat perspective.
choices.levelGoal: Add threat-informed testing to complement compliance testing. At least one threat-informed scenario accompanies each compliance cycle, compliance controls are mapped to ATT&CK, and a minimal scenario targets the most relevant threat actor.

choices.text: Testing is IOC-focused, e.g. vulnerability assessment, commodity tools
choices.tooltip: Commodity tools are off-the-shelf solutions that enable pen testing or red team activities using software that is well-known and easily detected.
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
recommendations: Build ATT&CK-mapped test scenarios for techniques used by your priority adversaries: Test whether defenses detect the underlying technique, not just known indicators. ATT&CK mapping enables coverage tracking over time.
Use CTI to prioritize which techniques to test: Focus on techniques actively observed in your sector. CTI-prioritized testing closes the most operationally relevant gaps first.
choices.levelGoal: Establish ATT&CK-mapped, technique-based test scenarios. Testing moves beyond specific indicators to test whether defenses detect the underlying techniques. Scenarios explicitly map to ATT&CK, enabling coverage tracking.

choices.text: Testing is behavior-focused, executing a single procedure of ATT&CK techniques
choices.tooltip: Most ATT&CK techniques have multiple procedures that accomplish the same behavior. For example, Scheduled Tasks can be accomplished through both schtasks.exe and the Task Scheduler.
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
choices.primaryOwner: Red Team Lead / Purple Team Lead
recommendations: Execute individual ATT&CK technique procedures informed by CTI adversary profiles: Single-procedure tests validate specific detection coverage with precision. Derive scenarios from CTI-built profiles of your priority threat actors.
Bring test findings into architecture decisions before controls are finalized: Testing that shapes what gets built is more valuable than testing that validates what already exists.
choices.levelGoal: Establish behavior-focused testing using individual ATT&CK technique procedures. Scenarios execute specific technique procedures informed by CTI adversary profiles. Coverage is tracked over time and findings inform defensive architecture decisions.

choices.text: Testing is behavior-focused, executing multiple procedures of a technique, perhaps using custom tooling
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
recommendations: Build multi-procedure, kill-chain-level adversary emulation scenarios: Full emulation requires linked technique chains executed with tooling that mirrors documented adversary behavior — not generic tooling EDR already catches.

Establish a formal test-to-improvement cycle: Build the documented pipeline from test finding to detection update, architectural change, and retesting. High-fidelity findings are only valuable if they drive systematic change.
choices.levelGoal: Establish adversary emulation capability with multi-procedure scenarios. Full kill-chain emulation is in place with custom tooling that mirrors documented adversary behavior. A formal test-to-improvement cycle ensures findings drive defensive changes.

questions.heading: Test Planning
questions.tooltip: Refer to Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) for deeper insight into aligning testing to the most impactful and likely threats.
questions.subheading: How are tests planned within your organization?

choices.text: Testing is designed to discover detection gaps and validate coverage for your attack surface
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
recommendations: Map test plans to specific attack surface components: Each test should reference which assets or entry points are in scope. Generic tests don't produce actionable coverage intelligence.
Maintain a coverage gap register: Testing reveals what's untested as much as what's vulnerable. Track gaps as a running list and link it to the test roadmap.
choices.levelGoal: Connect test planning explicitly to the attack surface. Test plans reference specific attack surface components, testing is prioritized by criticality, and coverage gaps are tracked through to remediation.

choices.text: Testing methodology is informed and prioritized by the threats and risks most relevant to your organization
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
recommendations: Establish a formal CTI briefing before each test planning cycle: CTI should review priority threat actors, active campaigns, and recent sector intelligence with the test team before plans are finalized.

Build a threat-to-test-scenario mapping and measure the coverage gap: For each priority threat actor, document which scenarios validate defenses against their TTPs. Track the percentage of CTI-identified priorities that are tested.
choices.levelGoal: Establish threat-informed test prioritization. CTI formally briefs the test team before each planning cycle. A threat-to-test-scenario mapping exists for priority threat actors and the coverage gap is measured.

choices.text: Testing is collaboratively planned with defenders, to include security response and remediation components
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
choices.primaryOwner: Red Team Lead / Purple Team Lead / SOC Director
recommendations: Formalize the collaborative planning process with IR and forensics included: Document who participates, what inputs are required, and what outputs are expected. Undocumented collaborative processes don't scale.

Build a formal intake process for test requests: SOC, detection engineering, and architecture should be able to formally submit testing needs. This shifts the program from internally-directed to demand-responsive.
choices.levelGoal: Establish collaborative test planning with defenders. The purple team process is formalized with defined participants and outputs. IR and forensics are included in planning. A formal intake process allows security teams to submit testing needs.

choices.text: Testing is linked to organizational metrics or key performance indicators (KPIs) to measure effectiveness in discovering gaps, validating coverage, and performing incident response and remediation
choices.tooltip: Example KPIs: time to initial access, time to detection, time from initial access to lateral movement, number of vulnerabilities identified, % of detection evasion, % of recommendations remediated
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy
recommendations: Connect test-derived metrics to security investment decisions: Test results that validate coverage — or identify gaps — are stronger justification for security budget than risk assessments alone.

Report testing maturity and coverage to the board: Board-level risk reporting should include what the test program has validated and where gaps remain. This positions testing as a strategic accountability mechanism.
choices.levelGoal: Link test planning to organizational metrics and KPIs. Test-derived metrics populate an executive dashboard, drive security budget decisions, and appear in board-level risk reporting.

questions.heading: Test Relevance
questions.subheading: How quickly is new CTI incorporated into your testing?

choices.text: Not CTI Driven or only relying on outdated CTI
choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy, Knowledge Sharing, Metrics
Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy, Knowledge Sharing, Metrics
recommendations: Establish standing intelligence requirements with the CTI team: Define the specific threat actors and technique categories the test program needs current intelligence on. This gives CTI a clear mandate.
Audit the test library for currency and define a freshness policy: Assess which scenarios are based on current intelligence. Document how old intelligence can be before a scenario must be updated.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a formal CTI-to-test connection with standing intelligence requirements. The test library is audited for CTI alignment, freshness requirements are defined, standing requirements are established with the CTI team, and alignment is formally measured.

choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy, Knowledge Sharing, Metrics
recommendations: Build a process for urgent test updates between monthly cycles: Define how quickly significant new intelligence must be reflected in the test queue and who has authority to reprioritize.
Move high-priority test scenarios to weekly CTI alignment: Those targeting your highest-priority adversaries should be reviewed against the latest intelligence each week.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve within-a-week CTI-to-test alignment. A process handles urgent test updates between monthly cycles. High-priority scenarios are on weekly CTI alignment. Velocity is measured and reported as a program health metric.

choices.red_team: Operational Planning and Selection, Work Management, Program Strategy, Knowledge Sharing, Metrics
recommendations: Maintain a dynamic test queue that can be reordered in real time: When critical intelligence arrives, reprioritize without an approval cycle. A lightweight process for same-day queue changes is the goal.

Jointly develop adversary emulation plans with the CTI team: CTI and test teams should co-author emulation plans based on jointly-analyzed threat actor profiles — not just consume intelligence reports.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve within-a-day CTI-to-test alignment with joint adversary emulation planning. Same-day test planning capability exists for critical intelligence. For adversary emulation scenarios, CTI and test teams jointly develop plans.

questions.heading: Test Triggers
questions.subheading: Are tests planned proactively or reactively?

choices.red_team: Process Continuous Improvement, Operational Approvals, Operational Planning and Selection
recommendations: Formalize post-incident testing protocols: Document who decides whether a test is warranted, what scope it covers, and what timeline it follows. Informal decisions produce inconsistent coverage.
Build a trigger catalog: Document the internal event types — breaches, detection gaps, architectural changes — that should trigger testing. This converts ad hoc decisions into a repeatable process.
choices.levelGoal: Establish documented protocols for internally-triggered testing. Post-incident testing defines ownership, scope, and timing. Testing scope extends beyond the specific attack vector. A trigger catalog defines which internal events warrant testing.

choices.red_team: Process Continuous Improvement, Operational Approvals, Operational Planning and Selection
recommendations: Define a watch list of external event types with SLA-governed testing responses: Sector advisories, actively-exploited CVEs, and campaign alerts should each have a defined testing response and initiation timeline.

Prioritize triggered tests by threat relevance and business impact: Not every external event warrants an immediate test. Document escalation criteria to distinguish high-urgency from standard-queue triggers.
choices.levelGoal: Establish documented protocols for externally-triggered testing. A watch list defines external event types that trigger tests. SLAs govern initiation time. Tests are prioritized by threat relevance and business impact.

choices.text: Testing is proactively planned on a periodic basis
choices.red_team: Process Continuous Improvement, Operational Approvals, Operational Planning and Selection
recommendations: Align the testing calendar to CTI review cycles: Schedule tests to incorporate the most recent intelligence. A test planned in isolation from current CTI validates last quarter's threat profile.
Synchronize test planning with the security roadmap: Schedule tests to validate controls before they go into production. Integrate test planning into architecture and change management processes.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a proactive testing calendar aligned to CTI review cycles. Tests are scheduled to incorporate the latest intelligence. The plan covers priority attack scenarios and is synchronized with the security roadmap.

choices.text: Testing is proactively planned on a continuous basis
choices.red_team: Process Continuous Improvement, Operational Approvals, Operational Planning and Selection
recommendations: Deploy automated security validation tooling for continuous coverage testing: Automated tools provide real-time detection gap visibility that periodic human-led tests cannot match. Scope carefully to avoid operational risk.

Differentiate continuous automated testing from periodic human-led exercises: Automated tools validate existing coverage; human-led exercises find novel gaps. Both are necessary — report on both to leadership.
choices.levelGoal: Establish continuous automated validation with differentiated human-led exercises. Automated tooling validates coverage continuously. Human-led exercises address complex and emergent gaps. Real-time dashboards report coverage, findings, and remediation status.

questions.heading: Test Results
questions.subheading: How do test results drive improvements in defensive measures?

choices.text: Actions are taken with internal security team to remediate individual hosts
choices.red_team: Program Knowledge Sharing, People Various Relationships, Operation Reporting
recommendations: Classify every finding as host-specific or systemic before assigning an owner: A finding requiring only a host patch is different from one revealing a detection, policy, or architecture gap. Misclassification routes findings to the wrong team.

Validate remediations by re-running the test technique: A finding marked 'fixed' should be confirmed by re-executing the original technique. Reported fixes that fail retesting are common — don't close findings without confirmation.
choices.levelGoal: Establish findings triage, systemic classification, and validated remediation. Findings are distinguished between host-specific and systemic gaps, routed to appropriate owners, and confirmed resolved by re-running the original technique before closure.

choices.text: Findings drive detection and architectural changes
choices.tooltip: Architectural changes improve the design of systems or networks to enhance security, e.g. strengthening key management, isolating critical subnets through network segmentation.
choices.red_team: Program Knowledge Sharing, People Various Relationships, Operation Reporting
choices.primaryOwner: Detection Engineering / Security Architecture / Red Team Lead
recommendations: Build a formal test-to-detection pipeline: Define how findings reach detection engineering — format, SLA, and tracking. Findings without a path to detection improvement are partly wasted.

Align finding severity to the organizational risk framework and hand off through GRC: Findings that don't map to organizational risk tiers won't be prioritized. Align severity ratings to GRC definitions so findings travel through standard risk management processes.
choices.levelGoal: Establish findings-driven detection and architecture pipelines with GRC-aligned handoff. A formal test-to-detection process routes findings to detection engineering. Handoff is documented with severity ratings aligned to the organization's risk framework. Retesting validates remediated findings.

choices.text: Findings drive organizational or policy changes
choices.tooltip: Organizational decisions are made based on the results of security testing, e.g. business strategy shifts, changes in hiring or training.
choices.red_team: Program Knowledge Sharing, People Various Relationships, Operation Reporting
recommendations: Build a findings-to-policy pipeline: Establish a formal process for findings that reveal policy gaps to be routed through governance with assigned owners and target dates.

Close the policy loop with retesting and build an organizational learning function: After a policy change, re-run the original test to confirm the intended effect. Route training needs and process failures identified by testing to the appropriate organizational functions.
choices.levelGoal: Establish findings-driven policy and organizational change. A structured findings-to-policy pipeline routes policy gaps through governance. Re-testing confirms policy changes had the intended effect. An organizational learning function routes training needs identified by testing.

name: Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) - Best Practices and Maturity Levels

questions.heading: Program Ownership
questions.subheading: Who is accountable for your organization’s continuous exposure management program, and what authority do they have to act across teams?

choices.text: No named owner. Exposure accountability is absent or informally distributed.
A lead exists — formally or informally — but without defined authority or scope to act across teams.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a named accountable lead for exposure management. The organization moves from no identified owner to a designated individual who holds the CTEM function — even if authority and scope are not yet formally defined.
recommendations: Name a CTEM lead immediately: Designate a specific individual responsible for continuous exposure management. Without a named owner, the program cannot emerge from ad hoc activities.
Define an initial scope of accountability: Document which assets, teams, and processes fall under the CTEM lead's purview. Even a rough scope creates the foundation for cross-team coordination.

choices.text: A named Director of CTEM or functional equivalent is designated with defined scope, escalation path, and CISO accountability.
choices.tooltip: Examples: Senior SecOps leader, purple team lead, detection engineering manager, or security program leader with cross-functional operational background.
choices.levelGoal: Designate a Director of CTEM or functional equivalent with defined scope, escalation path, and CISO accountability. The program has a real owner with enough authority and organizational positioning to act across teams.
recommendations: Formalize the CTEM role with a published charter: Document scope, decision-making authority, escalation paths, and CISO accountability in writing. Informal leads cannot direct cross-team action when priorities conflict.
Establish cross-team escalation rights: The CTEM owner needs documented authority to escalate unresolved coordination issues to the CISO. Without it, ownership exists only until the first conflict.

choices.text: The CTEM owner has documented cross-functional authority, with exposure outcomes formally integrated into enterprise governance and risk reporting.
choices.levelGoal: Establish documented cross-functional authority with exposure outcomes formally integrated into enterprise governance and board risk reporting. CTEM is a governed organizational capability, not just a security function.
recommendations: Document cross-functional authority in writing: Specify which teams the CTEM owner can direct, under what conditions, and what the escalation path is when coordination fails. Documented authority is enforceable authority.

Integrate exposure outcomes into enterprise governance and board risk reporting: CTEM metrics should appear in board risk reporting on a defined cadence. This integration makes CTEM a governance function, not just a security program.

questions.heading: Adversary Alignment
questions.subheading: To what extent does adversary behavior shape your CTEM program’s scope, validation scenarios, and cycle priorities?

choices.text: No adversary connection. Priorities are asset- or severity-driven.
Threat actors are identified at the industry level but do not shape scope or validation scenarios.
choices.levelGoal: Establish basic adversary awareness at the industry level. The organization identifies relevant threat actors in the sector but has not yet translated this awareness into program scope or validation priorities.
recommendations: Identify the 3–5 threat actor groups most likely to target your organization: Sector, geography, technology stack, and business model narrow the adversary set. A documented list is the minimum input for any adversary-aligned program.

Subscribe to sector-specific intelligence: ISAC membership, government advisories, and basic commercial CTI provide the foundation for adversary awareness. At this level, awareness is the goal — not yet active integration into program decisions.

choices.text: Scope, prioritization, and validation scenarios are explicitly mapped to TTPs of relevant adversaries.
choices.tooltip: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures — the behavioral fingerprint of how specific adversaries operate, as documented in MITRE ATT&CK.
choices.levelGoal: Explicitly map CTEM scope, prioritization, and validation scenarios to the TTPs of relevant adversaries. Adversary behavior shapes what gets tested and what gets prioritized — not just what gets monitored.
recommendations: Map CTEM scope and validation scenarios to adversary TTPs: For each priority threat actor, identify which ATT&CK techniques they use and ensure those techniques are covered in validation scenarios.

Use CTI to prioritize which attack paths to validate: Not all attack paths are equally likely. Adversary behavior intelligence determines which paths to validate first — making CTEM threat-informed rather than coverage-driven.

choices.text: Adversary behavior changes trigger scope and priority reviews within a defined timeframe.
choices.tooltip: Example: a new ransomware group targeting your sector triggers a scope review within 5 business days rather than waiting for the next scheduled cycle.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a defined timeframe within which adversary behavior changes trigger scope and priority reviews. The program responds to the threat landscape rather than waiting for scheduled cycles.
recommendations: Define a response timeframe for adversary behavior changes: Establish and document how quickly significant new adversary activity triggers a scope or priority review. The timeframe should be specific and measurable — 'promptly' is not a target.

Build a process for out-of-cycle scope and priority reviews: Responsive alignment requires the ability to trigger a focused CTEM pass outside the scheduled cadence. Define who initiates, what criteria apply, and what the minimum scope is.

choices.text: Adversary alignment is continuous. Emerging threat activity automatically surfaces in scope, prioritization, and validation.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve continuous adversary alignment where emerging threat activity automatically surfaces in scope, prioritization, and validation. The CTEM program and CTI function are operationally integrated.
recommendations: Integrate CTI feeds directly into CTEM scope and prioritization workflows: Emerging threat activity should surface automatically — not through manual analyst review of intelligence reports. Build or configure the integration that makes this possible.

Establish a continuous feedback loop from CTI to CTEM: When CTI identifies new adversary behavior, the mechanism should automatically update prioritization queues and flag scope changes. Manual escalation is a Level 3 capability — Level 4 requires automation.

questions.heading: Crown Jewel Scoping
questions.subheading: How are the assets and business processes most critical to your organization identified and maintained?

choices.text: High-value assets are informally understood but not formally documented or approved by executive stakeholders.
choices.levelGoal: Establish informal shared understanding of high-value assets. Key stakeholders agree on which assets matter most, even if that agreement is not documented or formally approved.
recommendations: Conduct a crown jewel identification session with security and business stakeholders: Even an informal workshop producing a list of the top 10 most critical assets is a meaningful starting point. Shared understanding is the goal.
Record the informal crown jewel list: Capture stakeholder consensus in a shared document. An undocumented list exists only in individuals' heads and cannot anchor program decisions.

choices.text: Crown jewels are formally documented, mapped to business impact, and carry CISO sign-off.
choices.tooltip: Assets and business processes where a breach would cause material harm — patient records, financial systems, operational technology, or other business-critical dependencies.
choices.levelGoal: Formally document crown jewels with business impact mapping and CISO sign-off. The organization has a governed, approved scope that can anchor CTEM prioritization and validation decisions.
recommendations: Formalize crown jewels with business impact mapping: For each designated crown jewel, document what business process it supports, the impact if compromised, and why it is materially critical. Informal understanding becomes a governed asset.

Obtain CISO sign-off on the crown jewel register: Executive endorsement transforms a security team list into an organizational priority. CISO accountability for the scope ensures CTEM prioritization has organizational backing.

choices.text: CTI informs crown jewel selection. Adversary targeting patterns shape which assets are designated.
choices.levelGoal: Add CTI-informed adversary targeting to the crown jewel designation process. Which assets are designated as crown jewels is shaped by who adversaries actually target — not just by business intuition.
recommendations: Incorporate CTI into the crown jewel designation process: Review adversary targeting intelligence alongside business impact assessments when designating crown jewels. Assets adversaries actively target warrant designation even if internal business impact alone might not prioritize them.
Map each crown jewel to the adversary groups most likely to target it: This mapping shapes which attack paths to validate and which TTP-based scenarios to include in the CTEM cycle.

choices.text: Scope is reviewed at least quarterly, or triggered by material changes to the threat landscape or business operations.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a quarterly review cadence with event-triggered reviews for material changes. Crown jewel scope is actively maintained rather than set once and forgotten.
recommendations: Establish a quarterly crown jewel review process with a defined agenda: Schedule reviews covering changes in adversary targeting, business operations, and third-party dependencies. The register should be current, not just comprehensive.

Define event triggers for out-of-cycle scope reviews: Material threat landscape changes, significant business changes (acquisitions, new products), or major third-party incidents should trigger a scope review outside the quarterly cadence.

choices.text: Scope adapts continuously. New adversary targeting, business changes, or third-party risk trigger near-real-time updates.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve continuous scope adaptation triggered by adversary targeting, business changes, and third-party risk. The crown jewel register responds to the threat landscape in near-real time.
recommendations: Build a continuous scope monitoring capability: Connect CTI feeds, business change notifications, and third-party risk signals to an automated process that flags potential crown jewel additions or changes in near-real time.

Establish clear decision criteria for continuous scope updates: Define what triggers an immediate scope update vs. a quarterly review item. Continuous monitoring without decision criteria produces noise, not action.

questions.heading: CTEM Cycle Cadence
questions.subheading: How does your organization operate the CTEM cycle (scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, mobilization)?

choices.text: No cycle. Exposure work is episodic, triggered by incidents, audits, or vendor advisories.
Some repeatable elements exist (e.g., scheduled scans) but the full end-to-end loop is not closed.
choices.levelGoal: Establish some repeatable elements of the CTEM cycle. The organization moves from purely episodic exposure work to at least one predictable, recurring activity — even if the full end-to-end loop is not yet closed.
recommendations: Map current exposure activities to the five CTEM stages: Identify which stages are currently operating — even episodically. Visibility into what exists is the prerequisite for closing the loop.

Connect existing exposure activities into a recognizable sequence: Link scheduled scans, vulnerability management work, and any validation activities into a documented workflow. An imperfect partial loop is better than episodic activities with no visible connection.

choices.text: A repeatable CTEM cycle operates end-to-end with a defined cadence, clear inputs and outputs, and adversary-relevance criteria at each pass.
choices.levelGoal: Operate a complete, end-to-end CTEM cycle with a defined cadence, clear inputs and outputs, and adversary-relevance criteria. All five stages — scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, mobilization — run as a connected loop.
recommendations: Define the full end-to-end CTEM cycle with owners, inputs, and outputs: Document all five stages, who owns each, what comes in from the prior stage, and what goes to the next. An undocumented cycle is an informal one.

Set a quarterly cycle cadence and commit to it: A quarterly end-to-end pass is a realistic starting target. The cadence creates accountability and a rhythm that enables other teams to plan around the program.

choices.text: The cycle is responsive. New adversary activity, disclosed vulnerabilities, or crown jewel changes can trigger a focused pass without waiting for the next scheduled run.
choices.levelGoal: Make the CTEM cycle responsive to new adversary activity, disclosures, and crown jewel changes. The organization can trigger a focused cycle pass without waiting for the next scheduled run.
recommendations: Build a process for triggering focused cycle passes: Define what events (new adversary campaign, critical CVE, crown jewel change) trigger an out-of-cycle pass, who initiates it, and what minimum scope it covers.

Distinguish focused passes from full-cycle runs: A responsive CTEM cycle doesn't re-run everything for every trigger. Define how focused passes are scoped to avoid creating unsustainable operational burden.

choices.text: The cycle is self-reinforcing and anticipatory. Each pass informs the next, and threat landscape changes automatically trigger targeted passes.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve a self-reinforcing, anticipatory CTEM cycle where each pass informs the next and threat changes automatically trigger targeted passes.
recommendations: Build the data flows that make cycles self-reinforcing: Prioritization outputs from each pass should automatically feed the next cycle's inputs. Remediation outcomes should adjust attack path density scores without manual recalibration.

Automate CTI-triggered cycle initiation: When relevant new adversary activity is identified, initiating a targeted pass should require minimal manual intervention. Define and implement the automation that closes this loop.

questions.heading: Exposure Prioritization
questions.subheading: What determines how your organization prioritizes exposures for remediation?

choices.text: CVSS score or vendor-assigned severity. Volume is the primary metric.
Contextual factors such as asset criticality or network reachability are applied, but inconsistently.
choices.levelGoal: Apply contextual factors to exposure prioritization. The organization moves beyond raw CVSS scores to apply asset criticality or network reachability — even if inconsistently.
recommendations: Apply asset criticality to every exposure before prioritizing: Add a criticality multiplier based on the asset tier of the affected system. Even a simple high/medium/low classification is a meaningful improvement over pure CVSS-based prioritization.

Add network reachability as a consistent prioritization factor: A vulnerability on an internet-facing system in a path to critical assets is more urgent than the same vulnerability on an isolated internal host. Build reachability into the prioritization workflow.

choices.text: Prioritization is based on validated attack path viability against defined crown jewels. Adversary-relevant paths are the focus.
choices.tooltip: Attack paths are validated when testing or adversary emulation confirms an attacker can chain weaknesses to reach a high-value asset and that defenses do not interrupt the path.
choices.primaryOwner: Director of CTEM / Red Team Lead
choices.levelGoal: Prioritize based on validated attack path viability against defined crown jewels. The focus shifts from severity to exploitability — which exposures create viable paths to your most critical assets.
recommendations: Validate attack paths before prioritizing exposures for remediation: Test whether exposures create viable end-to-end paths to crown jewels — not just whether individual vulnerabilities are theoretically exploitable. Validated path viability is the foundation of CTEM prioritization.

Focus the remediation queue on adversary-relevant paths to crown jewels: Filter the exposure backlog to prioritize chains that lead to your highest-value assets using techniques relevant to your priority adversaries. This is the core CTEM value proposition.

choices.text: Prioritization integrates CTI, validated attack paths, and adversary behavior in a consistent, documented, auditable workflow.
choices.levelGoal: Establish a consistent, documented, auditable prioritization workflow that integrates CTI, validated attack paths, and adversary behavior. Consistency and auditability are what separate a mature process from informed guesswork.
recommendations: Document and enforce a consistent prioritization workflow: Write down how CTI, validated attack paths, and adversary behavior combine to produce a prioritization decision. Consistency and auditability separate a mature process from informed guesswork.

Measure prioritization quality as a program metric: Track what percentage of remediations address validated attack paths to crown jewels vs. high-CVSS items not on critical paths. This demonstrates CTEM value over vulnerability management.

choices.text: Prioritization updates dynamically as adversary behavior and threat intel change. Cycle outcomes continuously refine rankings without manual recalibration.
choices.levelGoal: Achieve dynamic prioritization that updates automatically as adversary behavior and threat intelligence change, without manual recalibration. Cycle outcomes continuously refine rankings.
recommendations: Integrate CTI feeds and cycle outcomes directly into the prioritization engine: Dynamic prioritization requires that adversary behavior changes update priority rankings automatically — not through manual analyst review.

Build the remediation feedback mechanism: Confirmed closures should reduce attack path density scores; failed closures should re-enter the queue at elevated priority. The cycle should self-correct based on outcomes without manual intervention.

questions.heading: Remediation Execution
questions.subheading: How does your organization coordinate, execute, and verify remediation of confirmed exposures across teams?

choices.text: No defined remediation process. Exposures are handed off informally with no agreed timelines or ownership.
Ownership and SLAs exist but are not tied to exposure severity or crown jewel impact. Closures are assumed resolved without verification.
choices.tooltip: Re-testing can include vulnerability re-scan, control validation, or targeted adversary emulation confirming the specific attack path is no longer viable.
choices.levelGoal: Establish exposure ownership and SLAs. Confirmed exposures have named owners and agreed timelines — even if those timelines are not yet calibrated to exposure severity or crown jewel impact.
recommendations: Assign a named owner to every confirmed exposure: Each exposure exiting the CTEM cycle should have a documented owner in a remediation team. No owner means no accountability and no guarantee of action.
Establish SLAs for exposure remediation: Define target timelines and document them in the remediation workflow. Even broad initial SLAs create accountability where none existed.

choices.text: SLAs are tied to validated exposure severity and crown jewel impact. Cross-team coordination follows a documented workflow. Critical exposures are re-tested before closure.
choices.levelGoal: Tie SLAs to validated exposure severity and crown jewel impact, with documented cross-team coordination and re-testing of critical exposures before closure.
recommendations: Calibrate SLAs to validated exposure severity and crown jewel impact: Replace generic severity timelines with SLAs tied to the CTEM prioritization output — validated paths to crown jewels warrant the tightest timelines.
