Require re-testing of critical exposures before closure: High-priority exposures should not be marked closed on the remediation team's report alone. A targeted validation confirming the attack path is no longer viable is the closure standard.

choices.text: SLAs are consistently met. All closures require validation evidence. Exceptions are tracked and escalated through a defined process.
choices.levelGoal: Consistently meet SLAs with validation evidence required for all closures and a defined escalation process for exceptions. The program proves it is reliably reducing risk, not just tracking it.
recommendations: Track SLA compliance and make it visible to leadership: Build a dashboard showing SLA adherence rates by severity tier and crown jewel scope. Consistent visibility is the prerequisite for consistently meeting SLAs.

Formalize exception tracking and escalation: When SLAs are missed, the escalation path and management notification timeline should be documented and consistently followed. Exceptions without escalation create accountability gaps.

choices.text: Verification is integrated at scale. Validation outcomes confirm closure, feed back into the CTEM cycle, and continuously refine SLA targets.
choices.tooltip: Verification outcomes inform the next scoping and prioritization pass — confirmed closures reduce attack path density metrics; failed closures re-enter the prioritization queue.
choices.levelGoal: Integrate verification at scale with closure outcomes feeding back into the CTEM cycle to continuously refine SLA targets and reduce attack path density.
recommendations: Feed remediation verification outcomes back into the CTEM cycle: Confirmed closures should update attack path density metrics; failed closures should re-enter the prioritization queue at elevated priority. The cycle should self-correct based on outcomes.

Use closure rates to continuously refine SLA targets: SLAs consistently met may be too loose; ones consistently missed indicate a resourcing or process problem. Build a quarterly SLA review into CTEM governance.

questions.heading: Program Measurement
questions.subheading: What metrics does your organization use to measure CTEM program outcomes?

choices.text: Volume-based metrics: CVE counts, scan coverage, patch rates.
choices.levelGoal: Establish volume-based metrics as a starting point. CVE counts, scan coverage percentages, and patch rates create a measurement baseline even if they don't directly measure risk reduction.
recommendations: Establish baseline volume metrics and track them consistently: CVE counts, scan coverage percentages, and patch rates provide a starting baseline. A documented baseline enables improvement tracking over time.

Report metrics consistently on a defined cadence: Volume metrics only become useful when tracked over time. Establish a monthly or quarterly reporting format so trends are visible — even if the metrics don't yet tell the full story.

choices.text: Risk-adjusted metrics exist but reporting remains technical and tool-centric.
choices.levelGoal: Add risk-adjusted metrics. The organization moves beyond pure volume to metrics that incorporate risk context — even if reporting remains technically oriented.
recommendations: Add risk-adjusted metrics to the measurement set: Move from pure volume counts to metrics that incorporate context — exposure age weighted by asset criticality, remediation rates by severity tier. These are better leading indicators of risk reduction.

Begin translating technical metrics into risk language: Risk-adjusted metrics are the bridge between technical exposure management and business risk communication. Ensure at least one metric in the reporting set speaks to business risk, not just security operations.

choices.text: Metrics track attack path density, exposure trends, and validation outcomes against crown jewel scope.
choices.tooltip: Attack path density measures the number of viable paths an adversary could take to reach crown jewel assets. Reduction over time is the primary evidence of CTEM program effectiveness.
choices.levelGoal: Track attack path density, exposure trends, and validation outcomes against crown jewel scope. These metrics measure whether the CTEM program is reducing adversary success potential — not just managing exposure volume.
recommendations: Track attack path density as the primary CTEM effectiveness metric: Measure the number of viable paths an adversary could take to reach crown jewel assets. Reduction in attack path density over time is the primary evidence that CTEM is working.

Report validation outcomes against crown jewel scope: Track the percentage of prioritized exposures validated as genuinely exploitable and the percentage confirmed remediated. These outcomes measure whether the cycle is closing the right gaps.

choices.text: Exposure data actively informs executive and board-level decisions. CTEM outputs guide investment priorities, not just status updates.
choices.levelGoal: Establish exposure data as active input to executive and board-level decisions. CTEM metrics guide investment priorities rather than just reporting operational status.
recommendations: Build CTEM metrics into executive and board risk reporting: Exposure data should actively inform leadership investment priorities, not just report operational status to the security team.

Connect CTEM outputs to investment decisions: Track whether CTEM findings have changed priorities in the security budget or technology roadmap. If they haven't, the metrics are not yet driving organizational behavior.

choices.text: CTEM outcomes are integrated into enterprise risk posture. Metrics are tied to business resilience indicators and inform investment decisions.
choices.levelGoal: Integrate CTEM outcomes into enterprise risk posture. Metrics tie to business resilience indicators and inform investment decisions at the enterprise level.
recommendations: Integrate CTEM metrics with enterprise risk management: Connect attack path density, exposure trends, and validation outcomes to the organization's enterprise risk framework and board risk registers.

Tie CTEM outcomes to business resilience indicators: Translate attack path density and crown jewel exposure into business terms — operational continuity risk, data integrity risk, regulatory exposure — so metrics are meaningful to non-technical leadership.

questions.heading: Sector
questions.subheading: The organization's primary industry. Determines which threat actor groups and TTPs are most relevant to the profile.

questions.heading: Region
questions.subheading: Primary operating region. Shapes geopolitical threat exposure and applicable regulatory frameworks.

questions.heading: Annual Revenue
questions.subheading: Approximate annual revenue. Helps gauge organizational scale and attractiveness as a target for financially motivated threat actors.

questions.heading: Employee Headcount
questions.subheading: Total number of employees. Indicates attack surface breadth, identity sprawl, and the scale of insider risk exposure.

questions.heading: Regulatory Environment
questions.subheading: Compliance frameworks the organization is subject to (multi-select). Influences required controls, reporting obligations, and data types that must be protected.

questions.heading: Data Sensitivity
questions.subheading: Classifications of data the organization stores or processes (multi-select). Drives prioritization of crown jewel assets and shapes threat actor motivation profile.
